message.content:
Read ONE blog post in full and extract what it constrains about building an analytical data platform.

Fetch and convert it to text with exactly these commands:

  cd /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-adss-2026-09-07/45a0041f-5559-570b-bd39-1d1517807233/scratchpad/blog && curl -sSL --max-time 60 "https://blog.daana.dev/blog/definitions-for-integration" -o "definitions-for-integration.html" && node extract.js "definitions-for-integration.html" > "definitions-for-integration.txt" && wc -c "definitions-for-integration.txt"

Then read /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-adss-2026-09-07/45a0041f-5559-570b-bd39-1d1517807233/scratchpad/blog/definitions-for-integration.txt IN FULL with the Read tool (or cat). Do not skim, do not use WebFetch, do not summarize from the title. If the .txt is under 1500 characters the extraction failed — retry by running node extract.js on the raw html without the <article> isolation, or curl the page again.

Context you are serving: someone is about to BUILD the three-layer architecture this blog describes — DAS (data according to system), DAB (data according to business), DAR (data according to requirements) — using dlt for ingestion, a tool called daana-cli for the DAB focal model, and a generated Unified Star Schema for DAR. Your extraction is the only way this post reaches them. Be concrete and faithful.

Rules:
- mandates: only what the post actually says. Do not invent, do not generalize beyond the text.
- artifacts: anything NAMED — YAML keys, CLI commands and flags, schema names, table/column naming rules, SQL constructs, directory layouts, type mappings. Copy them verbatim. This is the highest-value field; be exhaustive.
- quotes: verbatim only, no paraphrase.
- openQuestions: places where the post says "you must decide X" or clearly leaves a choice open.
- If the post is an interview or company story with little build guidance, say so honestly via relevance:'low' and keep mandates short rather than padding.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

Published onThursday, May 28, 2026

# Why Definitions Are the Foundation of Every Data Warehouse

Authors- NamePatrik LagerTwitter

- The Definition Hierarchy

- Term: A Label, Not a Definition

- Concept: The Core of Integration

- Characteristic: Describing the Instance

- Domain: Where Values Come From

- Value: When Individual Entries Carry Meaning

- Instance: Where Definitions Meet Reality

- Acceptance: The Organizational Dimension

- Where This Leads

- Conclusion

Organizations rarely have just one source system. They have dozens - sometimes hundreds - spanning departments, divisions, and countries, each producing overlapping information under different names and structures. When they need to report across these boundaries, they build a Data Warehouse. But the Data Warehouse's primary job is not storage or performance or dashboards. It is Information Integration - creating a shared view of information that works regardless of where the data originated.

Integration has two sides: model integration (how we structure the common view) and semantic integration (what the information actually means). These are tightly intertwined, but semantic integration is where most teams struggle - and it is the focus of this article. Semantic integration depends on one foundational ingredient: Definitions.

Without clear Definitions, we cannot determine whether data from different systems refers to the same thing. Without that determination, there is no integration - just an expensive copy of source systems.

This is the first article in a three-part series. Here, we establish what Definitions are and why they form the foundation of any Data Warehouse. In Part 2, we apply this hierarchy to integration work in practice - how failure to have definitions can hurt the work of integration and much more. In Part 3, we explore how this integration discipline translates to declarative architectures and AI-driven platforms.

## The Definition Hierarchy

We need Definitions at four levels, each building on the previous one:

- `Concept` - What kind of thing are we describing?

- `Characteristic` - What properties describe instances of this Concept?

- `Domain` - What values can a Characteristic take?

- `Value` - What does a specific value within a Domain mean?

Two additional elements complete the picture: `Terms` (the labels we refer to Concepts by) and `Instances` (the individual things that fulfill a Concept's Definition). We will walk through each, starting with the most fundamental distinction - the difference between a name and a meaning.

## Term: A Label, Not a Definition

A Term is simply a name - a word or group of words that refers to a Concept. The Term "Car" by itself tells us nothing about what a car is. When someone says "I have a car," we understand only because we already carry a Definition of the Concept that the Term labels.

Terms are how we communicate, but they are not how we understand. A Term works as a "knowledge bearer" for those who already know the Definition behind it. For those who do not, it is meaningless - and communication about it becomes impossible.

In data warehousing, this plays out constantly. Two systems might use different Terms for the same Concept, or - more dangerously - the same Term for different Concepts. Without explicit Definitions, we cannot tell which case we are looking at.

## Concept: The Core of Integration

A Concept represents a "kind of thing." We naturally understand that every individual thing can be seen as an instance of some kind, and a Concept captures that abstraction. While the Concept itself never exists in the real world, it carries the Definition we rely on to sort and interpret information.

This is the central theme of Information Integration: finding commonality among information, regardless of where it was created in the organization. We do this by identifying shared Concepts and agreeing on their Definitions. How else would we know whether data from different source systems truly describes the same kind of thing?

A Concept's Definition should answer one question: What is that? The clearer the answer, the more reliable the integration. A poorly crafted Definition leads to incorrect groupings - records that look similar get integrated despite representing fundamentally different things.

This requirement for clear Definitions is what we call `Semantic Clarity` - the principle that every entity, attribute, relationship, and metric must have clear, business-oriented Definitions accessible to both humans and AI systems across the organization. Without it, ambiguity grows with scale, and integration becomes guesswork - for humans and AI systems alike.

## Characteristic: Describing the Instance

A Characteristic holds information that describes an instance of a Concept. If the Concept is "Customer," a Characteristic might be "Date of Birth." That value describes a specific customer, but it is not part of the Definition of "Customer" itself.

The key insight: `each Characteristic is its own Concept`. We need to define it independently because we need to know what data can legitimately populate it. This recursive principle - that each level in the hierarchy is itself a Concept requiring its own Definition - applies at every level from here on.

Consider "Bank Account" with the Characteristic "Account Balance." What does that actually mean? A simplified Definition: the balance at a specific point in time, representing the monetary value of settled transactions, not including accrued interest.

Without that Definition, we might load values that include unsettled transactions or accrued interest - mixing data with different meanings into the same field. Practitioners call this "mixing apples with pears," and it leads to reporting that looks correct but produces wrong conclusions.

## Domain: Where Values Come From

Each Characteristic draws its values from a Domain. There are two main types:

`Open Domains` require little integration effort. Date is a good example - "Date of Birth" takes values from the Date Domain. The values themselves do not need integration; only the format does.

`Closed Domains` often require significant integration work. A Domain, like every other level, is also a Concept and needs its own Definition. Consider "Account Balance Currency," which uses the Domain "ISO 4217 Currency Code" - a standardized set of values with its own Definition.

Values within a Domain also need a defined format. A date must follow its specified format regardless of how the source system stored it. Format integration is mechanical, but skipping it breaks downstream consistency.

## Value: When Individual Entries Carry Meaning

Individual Values can also represent their own Concepts. If we have a Concept "Organization" classified by the Global Industrial Classification System (GICS), one Value might be code "10" - the Term "Energy Sector," defined as:

`Companies whose businesses are dominated by the construction or provision of oil rigs, drilling equipment, energy-related services, or the exploration, production, marketing, refining, and transportation of oil, gas, coal, and other consumable fuels.

This Value, like the levels above it, is its own Concept with its own Definition. The same applies to ISO 4217 Currency Codes, where each code carries a Definition.

The ability to integrate Values - not just Concepts, Characteristics, and Domains - is what completes the common information view in the Data Warehouse.

## Instance: Where Definitions Meet Reality

An Instance is an individual thing that fulfills the Definition of a Concept - a specific bank account, a particular customer, an individual organization. The only way to determine whether something qualifies is to check it against the Concept's Definition.

Through the Values each Instance holds across its Characteristics, we can analyze and report. When the Concept, Characteristics, Domains, and Values are all integrated according to their Definitions, the information becomes usable throughout the organization - regardless of which system or country created it. That is the primary purpose of a Data Warehouse.

## Acceptance: The Organizational Dimension

The hierarchy above assumes Definitions already exist and are agreed upon. But agreed upon by whom, and at what scope?

A Definition's usability depends on how widely it is accepted. A Definition created for a single division cannot serve as an Enterprise Definition. This sounds obvious, but it is one of the most common problems in practice - expectations about data usability that exceed the scope of the Definitions behind it.

If someone claims an "Enterprise Data Warehouse," the Definitions must be accepted throughout the enterprise. They seldom are. This gap creates frustration, mistrust, and failed projects. Being explicit about acceptance scope - and honest about its limitations - is essential for realistic expectations.

## Where This Leads

The conceptual hierarchy above is the foundation, but it is only the starting point. These Definitions shape how both humans and AI systems work with data - from integration decisions and data modeling to platform construction. In Part 2, we look at how Definitions are applied in practice when doing integration work: where they break down, how teams negotiate them, and what happens when they are missing. In Part 3, we explore how this integration discipline translates into declarative architectures and AI-driven platforms.

## Conclusion

Information Integration is the discipline of determining which Concept each data record belongs to. The only way to do this reliably is through Definitions at every level:

- `Concept Definition` - what kind of thing is this?

- `Characteristic Definition` - what describes instances of this Concept?

- `Domain Definition` - what values are valid, and in what format?

- `Value Definition` - what does a specific value mean?

The organizational challenge is just as real as the technical one. Definitions need broad acceptance to deliver their promised scope, and that acceptance is hard-won. But the investment compounds: Semantic Clarity - every Concept, Characteristic, Domain, and Value clearly defined and broadly accepted - creates a foundation that the rest of the organization can build on.

Where to start? Before integrating data from two systems, write down the Definition of each shared Concept and verify that both teams agree on it. If they do not, you have found the exact place where integration will break.

For a deeper treatment of Definitions and their management - including formal methods for creating, validating, and governing them across an organization - see Definitions in Information Management by Malcolm D. Chisholm, Ph.D. It remains one of the clearest formal frameworks on this subject.

input.thesis: A Data Warehouse's primary job is Information Integration, not storage, performance, or dashboards — and integration has two sides, model integration and semantic integration, of which semantic integration is the hard one. Semantic integration rests entirely on Definitions, organized as a recursive hierarchy: Concept, Characteristic, Domain, Value (plus Terms as labels and Instances as the things that fulfill a Concept's Definition), where every level is itself a Concept needing its own Definition. mandates.claim: "the Data Warehouse's primary job is not storage or performance or dashboards. It is Information Integration - creating a shared view of information that works regardless of where the data originated."
mandates.implication: The platform's success criterion is a shared, source-independent view of information — not pipeline throughput, model count, or dashboard delivery. Ingestion (dlt/DAS) and star-schema generation (DAR) are means; the integrated common view is the deliverable.

mandates.claim: "Without clear Definitions, we cannot determine whether data from different systems refers to the same thing. Without that determination, there is no integration - just an expensive copy of source systems."
mandates.implication: A source-shaped landing layer is explicitly NOT integration. Building DAS alone (dlt loading each system's structure) produces the 'expensive copy' the post warns about; the integration verdict is made in the business layer against Definitions.

mandates.claim: Integration has two sides: model integration (how we structure the common view) and semantic integration (what the information actually means); these are tightly intertwined, but semantic integration is where most teams struggle.
mandates.implication: Generating a Unified Star Schema is model integration only. It does not by itself produce integration — the semantic side must be carried explicitly alongside the structure, or the generated model is structurally clean and semantically hollow.

mandates.claim: "A Concept's Definition should answer one question: What is that?" and "A poorly crafted Definition leads to incorrect groupings - records that look similar get integrated despite representing fundamentally different things."
mandates.implication: Every entity in the focal model needs a stored Definition that answers 'What is that?', and that Definition — not structural resemblance between source tables — is what authorizes merging two sources into one entity.

mandates.claim: Semantic Clarity is defined as "the principle that every entity, attribute, relationship, and metric must have clear, business-oriented Definitions accessible to both humans and AI systems across the organization."
mandates.implication: Definitions are required on four object kinds — entity, attribute, relationship, AND metric — not just entities; they must be business-oriented (not technical restatements of column names) and machine-accessible, i.e. stored inside the model artifacts rather than in an external wiki. Note the hierarchy in the article covers Concept/Characteristic/Domain/Value but never names a metric level.

mandates.claim: "The key insight: each Characteristic is its own Concept. We need to define it independently because we need to know what data can legitimately populate it. This recursive principle - that each level in the hierarchy is itself a Concept requiring its own Definition - applies at every level from here on."
mandates.implication: Attributes are first-class definable objects, not annotations on a parent entity. The focal model must support a Definition per attribute, per domain, and per value — the same definition machinery applied recursively at each level.

mandates.claim: A Characteristic holds information that describes an instance of a Concept, but "it is not part of the Definition of 'Customer' itself" (e.g. Concept 'Customer', Characteristic 'Date of Birth').
mandates.implication: Keep the entity's Definition separate from its attribute list; the Definition must not be written as an enumeration of its columns.

mandates.claim: The worked example: Concept "Bank Account", Characteristic "Account Balance", defined as "the balance at a specific point in time, representing the monetary value of settled transactions, not including accrued interest." Without that Definition "we might load values that include unsettled transactions or accrued interest - mixing data with different meanings into the same field."
mandates.implication: The attribute Definition is the acceptance test for which source field may populate it. Source-to-target mapping decisions must be justified against the attribute's Definition, and a source field whose meaning differs (settled vs unsettled, with vs without accrued interest) must not land in that attribute even if names match.

mandates.claim: "Each Characteristic draws its values from a Domain," and a Domain "like every other level, is also a Concept and needs its own Definition." Two main types: Open Domains "require little integration effort"; Closed Domains "often require significant integration work."
mandates.implication: Domain is a modelled object attached to each characteristic, carrying its own Definition, and classified as open or closed — the classification predicts where integration effort lands. Closed-domain characteristics (code lists) need value-level integration work planned; open-domain ones (Date) need only format work.

mandates.claim: "Values within a Domain also need a defined format. A date must follow its specified format regardless of how the source system stored it. Format integration is mechanical, but skipping it breaks downstream consistency."
mandates.implication: Format normalization on the way from source structure to the business model is mandatory, not optional, and the target format is a property of the Domain — the source system's storage format never wins.

mandates.claim: Individual Values can be their own Concepts with their own Definitions (GICS code "10" = Term "Energy Sector" with a full prose definition; "The same applies to ISO 4217 Currency Codes, where each code carries a Definition"), and "The ability to integrate Values - not just Concepts, Characteristics, and Domains - is what completes the common information view in the Data Warehouse."
mandates.implication: Reference/code tables must carry a per-value Definition, and cross-system code values must be integrated to a common set. Stopping integration at the entity/attribute level leaves the common view incomplete.

mandates.claim: "A Term is simply a name... Terms are how we communicate, but they are not how we understand." "Two systems might use different Terms for the same Concept, or - more dangerously - the same Term for different Concepts. Without explicit Definitions, we cannot tell which case we are looking at."
mandates.implication: Never integrate on name match. Automated or AI-assisted mapping that aligns source columns by label is exactly the failure mode described; the model must keep Term (label) and Definition (meaning) as separate fields so a Term collision can be detected.

mandates.claim: "An Instance is an individual thing that fulfills the Definition of a Concept... The only way to determine whether something qualifies is to check it against the Concept's Definition."
mandates.implication: The predicate deciding which source rows become instances of a business entity (filters, row-level selection criteria) must be derivable from and traceable to that entity's Definition.

mandates.claim: "A Definition's usability depends on how widely it is accepted. A Definition created for a single division cannot serve as an Enterprise Definition." "If someone claims an 'Enterprise Data Warehouse,' the Definitions must be accepted throughout the enterprise. They seldom are."
mandates.implication: Acceptance scope is metadata that belongs with each Definition, and the scope a deliverable is advertised at must not exceed the scope of the Definitions behind it. Being "explicit about acceptance scope - and honest about its limitations - is essential for realistic expectations."

mandates.claim: "Where to start? Before integrating data from two systems, write down the Definition of each shared Concept and verify that both teams agree on it. If they do not, you have found the exact place where integration will break."
mandates.implication: Definition-writing and cross-team agreement precede the integration build for each shared Concept; disagreement is a discovered risk to surface, not a blocker to route around.

mandates.claim: When Concept, Characteristics, Domains, and Values "are all integrated according to their Definitions, the information becomes usable throughout the organization - regardless of which system or country created it. That is the primary purpose of a Data Warehouse."
mandates.implication: All four levels must be integrated for the result to count — partial integration (entities only, or entities plus attributes) does not reach the stated goal.

mandates.implication: Every entity in the focal model needs a stored Definition that answers 'What is that?', and that Definition — not structural resemblance between source tables — is what authorizes merging two sources into one entity.

mandates.claim: Semantic Clarity is defined as "the principle that every entity, attribute, relationship, and metric must have clear, business-oriented Definitions accessible to both humans and AI systems across the organization."
mandates.implication: Definitions are required on four object kinds — entity, attribute, relationship, AND metric — not just entities; they must be business-oriented (not technical restatements of column names) and machine-accessible, i.e. stored inside the model artifacts rather than in an external wiki. Note the hierarchy in the article covers Concept/Characteristic/Domain/Value but never names a metric level.

mandates.claim: "The key insight: each Characteristic is its own Concept. We need to define it independently because we need to know what data can legitimately populate it. This recursive principle - that each level in the hierarchy is itself a Concept requiring its own Definition - applies at every level from here on."
mandates.implication: Attributes are first-class definable objects, not annotations on a parent entity. The focal model must support a Definition per attribute, per domain, and per value — the same definition machinery applied recursively at each level.

mandates.claim: A Characteristic holds information that describes an instance of a Concept, but "it is not part of the Definition of 'Customer' itself" (e.g. Concept 'Customer', Characteristic 'Date of Birth').
mandates.implication: Keep the entity's Definition separate from its attribute list; the Definition must not be written as an enumeration of its columns.

mandates.claim: The worked example: Concept "Bank Account", Characteristic "Account Balance", defined as "the balance at a specific point in time, representing the monetary value of settled transactions, not including accrued interest." Without that Definition "we might load values that include unsettled transactions or accrued interest - mixing data with different meanings into the same field."
mandates.implication: The attribute Definition is the acceptance test for which source field may populate it. Source-to-target mapping decisions must be justified against the attribute's Definition, and a source field whose meaning differs (settled vs unsettled, with vs without accrued interest) must not land in that attribute even if names match.

mandates.claim: "Each Characteristic draws its values from a Domain," and a Domain "like every other level, is also a Concept and needs its own Definition." Two main types: Open Domains "require little integration effort"; Closed Domains "often require significant integration work."
mandates.implication: Domain is a modelled object attached to each characteristic, carrying its own Definition, and classified as open or closed — the classification predicts where integration effort lands. Closed-domain characteristics (code lists) need value-level integration work planned; open-domain ones (Date) need only format work.

mandates.claim: "Values within a Domain also need a defined format. A date must follow its specified format regardless of how the source system stored it. Format integration is mechanical, but skipping it breaks downstream consistency."
mandates.implication: Format normalization on the way from source structure to the business model is mandatory, not optional, and the target format is a property of the Domain — the source system's storage format never wins.

mandates.claim: Individual Values can be their own Concepts with their own Definitions (GICS code "10" = Term "Energy Sector" with a full prose definition; "The same applies to ISO 4217 Currency Codes, where each code carries a Definition"), and "The ability to integrate Values - not just Concepts, Characteristics, and Domains - is what completes the common information view in the Data Warehouse."
mandates.implication: Reference/code tables must carry a per-value Definition, and cross-system code values must be integrated to a common set. Stopping integration at the entity/attribute level leaves the common view incomplete.

mandates.claim: "A Term is simply a name... Terms are how we communicate, but they are not how we understand." "Two systems might use different Terms for the same Concept, or - more dangerously - the same Term for different Concepts. Without explicit Definitions, we cannot tell which case we are looking at."
mandates.implication: Never integrate on name match. Automated or AI-assisted mapping that aligns source columns by label is exactly the failure mode described; the model must keep Term (label) and Definition (meaning) as separate fields so a Term collision can be detected.

mandates.claim: "An Instance is an individual thing that fulfills the Definition of a Concept... The only way to determine whether something qualifies is to check it against the Concept's Definition."
mandates.implication: The predicate deciding which source rows become instances of a business entity (filters, row-level selection criteria) must be derivable from and traceable to that entity's Definition.

mandates.claim: "A Definition's usability depends on how widely it is accepted. A Definition created for a single division cannot serve as an Enterprise Definition." "If someone claims an 'Enterprise Data Warehouse,' the Definitions must be accepted throughout the enterprise. They seldom are."
mandates.implication: Acceptance scope is metadata that belongs with each Definition, and the scope a deliverable is advertised at must not exceed the scope of the Definitions behind it. Being "explicit about acceptance scope - and honest about its limitations - is essential for realistic expectations."

mandates.claim: "Where to start? Before integrating data from two systems, write down the Definition of each shared Concept and verify that both teams agree on it. If they do not, you have found the exact place where integration will break."
mandates.implication: Definition-writing and cross-team agreement precede the integration build for each shared Concept; disagreement is a discovered risk to surface, not a blocker to route around.

mandates.claim: When Concept, Characteristics, Domains, and Values "are all integrated according to their Definitions, the information becomes usable throughout the organization - regardless of which system or country created it. That is the primary purpose of a Data Warehouse."
mandates.implication: All four levels must be integrated for the result to count — partial integration (entities only, or entities plus attributes) does not reach the stated goal.

quotes: But the Data Warehouse's primary job is not storage or performance or dashboards. It is Information Integration - creating a shared view of information that works regardless of where the data originated.

Without clear Definitions, we cannot determine whether data from different systems refers to the same thing. Without that determination, there is no integration - just an expensive copy of source systems.

This requirement for clear Definitions is what we call Semantic Clarity - the principle that every entity, attribute, relationship, and metric must have clear, business-oriented Definitions accessible to both humans and AI systems across the organization.

The key insight: each Characteristic is its own Concept. We need to define it independently because we need to know what data can legitimately populate it. This recursive principle - that each level in the hierarchy is itself a Concept requiring its own Definition - applies at every level from here on.

Values within a Domain also need a defined format. A date must follow its specified format regardless of how the source system stored it. Format integration is mechanical, but skipping it breaks downstream consistency.
The ability to integrate Values - not just Concepts, Characteristics, and Domains - is what completes the common information view in the Data Warehouse.
A Definition's usability depends on how widely it is accepted. A Definition created for a single division cannot serve as an Enterprise Definition.

Before integrating data from two systems, write down the Definition of each shared Concept and verify that both teams agree on it. If they do not, you have found the exact place where integration will break.
openQuestions: The post asks its own unanswered question about acceptance: "The hierarchy above assumes Definitions already exist and are agreed upon. But agreed upon by whom, and at what scope?" It insists scope be explicit but never says how to record or govern it — a builder must decide the representation (a scope field per definition? per model? an approver list?).

How Definitions are made "accessible to both humans and AI systems" is asserted as a requirement but never specified — no format, storage location, key name, or serialization is given. The DAB focal model's definition-carrying mechanism is entirely a builder choice.

Semantic Clarity requires definitions on "entity, attribute, relationship, and metric," but the four-level hierarchy (Concept / Characteristic / Domain / Value) contains no relationship or metric level. How relationships and metrics fit the hierarchy — and what their Definitions must answer — is left open.

Domains need "a defined format," but no format-specification syntax, type system, or DAS→DAB type-mapping rule is offered. Where format normalization executes (dlt ingestion vs. the business layer) is unresolved.

Open vs Closed is presented as "two main types" of Domain with hedged language ("require little" / "often require significant"), implying other types exist and that the classification may not be a clean binary flag.

The post says definition disagreement between two teams locates "the exact place where integration will break" but gives no resolution procedure — whether to split into separate Concepts, escalate, or narrow the acceptance scope is undecided.

Whether Value-level integration means mapping every source code to a shared standard (ISO 4217, GICS) or defining a bespoke common Domain per Concept is not settled; only that Values must be integrated.

The post never mentions DAS, DAB, DAR, dlt, daana-cli, or the Unified Star Schema. The mapping from this hierarchy onto a three-layer declarative architecture is explicitly deferred to Part 3 ("how this integration discipline translates into declarative architectures and AI-driven platforms").
